## How git worktrees work

A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository in a different directory. Every worktree shares one `.git` database, so commits, branches, and stashes are visible everywhere. Each worktree holds its own working files and its own `HEAD`.

- Git allows a branch to be checked out in only one worktree at a time.
- Creating a worktree costs a directory of files, not a full clone.
- Deleting a worktree folder does not delete its branch. Run `git worktree prune` to clear stale entries.

```bash
# Create a worktree on a new branch, based on main
git worktree add ../demo-fix -b fix/typo main

# List every checkout and the branch it holds
git worktree list

# Remove the worktree when finished (branch stays)
git worktree remove ../demo-fix
```

| Task | Without worktrees | With worktrees |
|---|---|---|
| Review a PR while your feature branch has uncommitted work | Stash, switch, switch back | Open a second directory |
| Run a long build on `main` | Blocks your editor's branch | Runs in its own folder |
| Compare two branches side by side | Two clones | One repo, two folders |

Use worktrees when you need two branches open at once. Plain branch switching is enough for quick, sequential work.

# The last watch

Iris Calloway had kept the Harrow Point light for nineteen years, and in all that time the sea never asked her a question. It came in and went out. The light turned every eleven seconds. She counted them the way other people counted breaths.

The automation crew arrived in March. Two men in orange vests, a tablet with a green progress bar, and a helicopter that hovered over the rocks like a nervous insect. They told her the station would run itself by autumn. They were polite about it. One of them, a young man named Teo, asked whether she would like a plaque.

"For what?" she said.

"For the service."

She looked at him for a while. Then she made the coffee the way her mother had, in the dented steel pot that was older than the lamp.

Now it was October, and the crew had gone. The new controller hummed in the lantern room, a gray box bolted to the iron where her logbook used to sit. Every night she checked it. Every night it reported normal. Every night she felt slightly more useless, which she had not expected.

On the ninth night the fog came in thick. The horn sounded from the bell buoy, stopped, then sounded again. The controller displayed a fault code she didn't recognize. Iris stood with one hand on the cold glass and listened.

Somewhere past the reef, a small boat was coming home late. She could hear its engine, thin and uncertain, rising and falling with the swell. The fishing boats from the village always came back this way in fog. Her husband had been one of them. He came home in fog for twenty-two years, until the night he didn't.

The controller said everything was fine. It was probably right. The light was turning, the lens was clean, and the mechanism had no reason to fail.

But the boat did not know that. It needed to see a light where a light should be, and the lens could only give it one if someone kept it honest.

Iris went down the iron stairs, counting the steps out of habit. In the storeroom she found the old manual crank for the backup shutter, the one nobody had oiled in a decade. She worked grease into it with a rag. Her knuckles ached. She didn't stop.

Then she climbed back up, sat beside the controller, and did the one thing it could not do. She watched the fog. When the engine noise drifted closer, she flashed the spare lamp toward the sound, slow and steady: three long and one short. It was the signal her husband had taught her, the one that meant *come home*.

It took forty minutes. At the end, a red and green hull slid into the harbor mouth, and a man on the deck raised an arm.

Iris set the lamp down. Her hands shook. She poured the cold coffee into her mug anyway and drank it standing, looking out at the water.

In the morning she wrote in the paper logbook that nobody had asked her to keep. *Fog. Boat home. Light held.* Then she underlined the last two words twice, the way you mark something you intend to remember.

messages.text: Write a 700 word story about a lighthouse keeper, in 8 paragraphs. No tools.

**The Keeper of Gull Rock**

Halvorsen had kept the light on Gull Rock for thirty years. The sea had never once asked him for anything it did not take. He wound the clockwork every four hours and trimmed the wick at dusk. He logged the weather in a hand his late wife had called a doctor's, only worse. The beam swept the water, and ships steered by it without ever learning his name.

The supply boat came on the first Tuesday of each month, and that was the only day he spoke to anyone who was not a gull. This month it brought a young man named Teodor, sent from the mainland office to look at the failing motor and to tell Halvorsen what everyone already knew. The automatic system was coming. Within a year the rock would run itself from a desk three hundred miles away.

Halvorsen did not argue. He showed Teodor the brass gears, the lens with its thousand prisms, and the shelf of logbooks going back to 1961. Teodor typed everything into a tablet. He asked why the keeper climbed the stairs by hand when the lift could do it. Halvorsen said the stairs were the only exercise he got, and that no lift had ever been checked by a man who knew where the fog came from.

That night the fog arrived faster than the forecast. It rolled over the water thick as wool, and within minutes the horn on the north side was the only sound left. Halvorsen sent Teodor up to the lamp room with a flashlight and a list. The young man climbed too fast, and Halvorsen heard him swear on the third landing. Teodor was not built for this yet. Neither had Halvorsen been, his first winter.

The motor failed at eleven. The lamp stopped turning, and the beam hung fixed in the fog like a bruise. Halvorsen went up with a hand crank he had made from an old bicycle gear and set it against the housing. Teodor held the lantern. Their breath came out white in the cold room, and the crank groaned with every turn. "Keep it steady," Halvorsen said. The boy did, for two hours, until his hands cramped, and he never once complained.

Somewhere past two in the morning, Teodor asked why he had stayed. Halvorsen did not answer right away. He was watching the beam, which had started turning again, slowly and then faster. Somewhere to the east a fishing boat was counting the flashes and matching them to its chart. "Out there somebody is steering by a light they never think about," he said. "Somebody has to be that light."

The fog lifted at dawn the way it always did, all at once, as if someone had pulled a sheet off the sea. Halvorsen saw the boat first, a small trawler with its running lights still burning, and then the whole grey harbor came into focus. The skipper raised one hand from the wheelhouse. Halvorsen raised his back. It was not thanks, exactly. Fishermen did not thank lights. But it was the same thing.

Teodor filed his report that afternoon. He recommended replacing the motor, and he wrote that the keeper should be consulted on any further decisions. He did not mention the crank. Halvorsen read the report at the kitchen table, found the sentence about consultation, and underlined it twice in pencil. Then he climbed the stairs by hand to wind the clock, the way he always had.

Mara Okonkwo had kept the light at Hollis Rock for eleven years, and the lamp had never gone dark on her watch. She wound the clockwork every four hours, polished the lens on Tuesdays, and logged the weather in a ledger that nobody read. The ledger was the job, as far as the government was concerned. The light was the job, as far as she was concerned. Nobody on the mainland had asked her opinion about either.

The letter arrived in March. A solar beacon would replace the station by autumn, a steel post bolted to the reef two hundred yards offshore. It would blink on its own schedule and never need winding. The letter thanked her for her service in the careful language of people who had never climbed the one hundred and twelve steps. She read it twice at the kitchen table, then slid it into the ledger between the pages for April. She was not angry. She felt more like someone left behind in a room after the party had moved on.

In May the fog sat on the water for nine days straight. Mara climbed the stairs every four hours anyway, because fog was the reason the light existed. Ships could not see the rocks, so they listened for the horn and watched for the beam. Her boots were already wet from the landing, and the salt got into everything. On the fourth night she heard an engine idling somewhere to the west, low and uncertain, a boat that had lost its bearings. She wound the clock, lit the lamp, and leaned on the horn lever until her forearms burned.

The engine found the channel a little before two in the morning. Mara watched its running light slide north past the rocks, slow once, then pick up speed and vanish into the grey. Nobody aboard would ever learn her name. She had made her peace with that years ago, after realizing her father kept the light at the Dunes for thirty years and could not name half the crews he saved. The job had never been about the names.

The skipper's son rowed out the next morning with a crate of lobsters and a note sealed in a plastic bag. The boy was maybe nineteen and kept his eyes on the lobsters the whole time. The note said only, "You were the only thing we could see." Mara read it twice on the landing. She took the crate. She kept the note, filed it in the ledger under May, next to the fog.

The beacon went up in October on a grey morning. A tender boat brought two men in orange jackets, and they bolted the new post to the reef in under an hour. Mara watched from the gallery with her arms folded. When the men were gone, the light began to blink, clean and white, every six seconds, with nobody touching it. It was more reliable than she had ever been. She did not enjoy admitting that, so she did not admit it to anyone, including the ledger.

Her last shift fell on a Thursday with no fog and a flat, calm sea. The old lamp still worked, and nobody had asked her to light it. Nobody would notice if she didn't. She climbed the one hundred and twelve steps anyway, the way she always had, and wound the clockwork until the weights hung at the bottom of their shaft. She lit the lamp and watched the beam go round over water that did not need it. It was the purest part of the job, and nobody needed it anymore.

At dawn she polished the lens one last time, locked the iron door, and started down. She counted the steps out loud, the way she had on her first morning, and at the bottom she did not look back. Behind her the new beacon kept blinking, faithful and asking nothing. Mara walked the causeway toward the mainland with her hands loose at her sides, lighter than she had been in eleven years. She could not decide whether that was relief or grief, so she let it be both.

Marguerite Hale kept the light on Vesper Rock for thirty-one years, and in all that time the sea never once asked her permission. She climbed the 112 iron steps every dusk with a tin of paraffin under one arm. The ships out there would never see her face. They would see the beam and trust it, and that trust was the whole job. She did not mind being invisible. She minded when the beam failed.

The winter the relief boat stopped coming, the clockwork that turned the lens seized in November. She wound it by hand every four hours through the dark, forearms burning, counting turns the way her mother had counted rosary beads. Nobody ordered her to do it. The rock sat a mile from the nearest town, and the board had stopped answering her letters in October. The light was hers to keep, so she kept it.

In the third week of February, a fishing smack named the *Ada Lynn* drifted toward the reef at the edge of her sight. She watched its lantern wobble, then stop. Marguerite grabbed the signal flags, though no one aboard could read them through that sleet. Instead she hauled on the fog bell rope and rang it until her palms split and the rope went slick. Ring, pause, ring. That was all the bell could say.

Hours passed. The bell kept going, and her shoulders stopped reporting pain somewhere past eleven. Near midnight a boy's voice came thin across the water, then another, and she understood they were steering toward the sound. She had never thought of the bell as something a person could follow from a pitching deck. She rang it harder and kept one eye on the water in case the lamp needed her too.

Morning brought a grey calm. Four men stood on the landing, soaked and shaking, and the youngest, maybe fourteen, asked her why she hadn't gone to bed. She told him the truth. The lamp had to be lit, the bell had to be rung, and nobody else was coming to do either. He nodded slowly, as though that were a reasonable answer, and it was. She gave them tea from the storm kettle and watched the smack limp off toward the harbor.

The relief boat finally arrived in March with a new mechanic and a sack of letters from the lighthouse board. The letters praised her service in the stiff language of officials who had never climbed the stairs. One promised her record would be forwarded. Another suggested she consider retirement, given her age, as if she had not been awake for three days straight. She read them on the step and folded them into her coat pocket, unsure whether she felt insulted or only tired.

What she wanted was smaller. She wanted someone to ask whether the lens had cracked in the storm, or whether damp was creeping into the oil store. Nobody asked. A month later a parcel came out on the supply run: a salted cod wrapped in newspaper, with a pencil note that read, "Thanks for the noise. Tom." She tacked the note above the stove, beside the barometer. Of all the paper that reached her that year, it was the only letter she trusted.

She stayed on the rock until the spring of her thirty-second year, when her knees finally refused the stairs. On her last evening she climbed up one more time and wound the clockwork by hand. She watched the beam sweep across the black water, slow and steady, the way it had every night for thirty-one years. Somewhere out there a ship she would never see was steering by it. She went down the steps without looking back, and for once she let the light run on without her.

**The Keeper of Kessock Point**

Arthur Penhale had kept the light at Kessock Point for thirty-one years, and the sea had never once asked him for anything he could refuse. It asked for paraffin. It asked for wicks trimmed at dusk and the lens polished before the salt dried on it. Every morning he climbed the one hundred and fourteen iron steps, counting them out of habit, and wrote the weather in the log in a hand that had shrunk a little each decade. Nobody read the log. That was the point of it.

The autumn his wife Maud died, the relief boat stopped coming. The Board wrote that the route was no longer economic and that an automated beacon would be fitted by spring. Spring came. The beacon did not. Penhale kept the light alone through the winter, and by January he had started sleeping in the chair beside the lamp room, because the stairs had begun to feel longer than they used to. He told himself this was practical. He knew it was not entirely practical.

In February a fishing boat out of the south harbour went missing in fog. Penhale heard the engine before he saw anything, an uneven thump drifting in from the water west of the rocks. His radio had died in December. What he had was a foghorn that wheezed, a brass bell, and a lamp that could be turned faster than it was built to turn. He wound the clockwork by hand, both arms working the crank until his shoulders burned, and he rang the bell until the rope tore a strip of skin from his palm. He did not stop to bind it. Stopping was not an option.

Morning came grey and flat. The boat lay on the shingle at the bottom of the cove, its bow stove in, and three men stood on the rocks above it. One of them was waving. They had steered by the flashes, they told him later, and had been sure for an hour that the light was a ship coming to meet them. Penhale had not known the lamp reached so far. He had always assumed nobody was looking up.

The Board's letter arrived in April. It thanked him for his long service and noted that Kessock Point had been reclassified as a light of secondary importance. A relief keeper would be assigned in the autumn. Penhale read the letter twice at the kitchen table, then folded it into the log book between the pages for February. He did not feel triumphant. He felt tired, which was new, and oddly he was glad of it.

Ilse Varga came over on the first boat of summer. She was the young clerk from the mainland office, and she arrived with a case of books and a bicycle she had no use for on an island with one road. She was not what he expected. She asked to see the logs, and she read them standing up, turning each page by its edge so the paper would not crease. At the end she looked up and asked why he had recorded the water temperature every single day for thirty years when no one had required it.

"Habit," he said. Then, because that was not quite true: "Maud liked to know whether the sea was cold."

**The Keeper of Kessock Point**

Arthur Penhale had kept the light at Kessock Point for thirty-one years, and the sea had never once asked him for anything he could refuse. It asked for paraffin. It asked for wicks trimmed at dusk and the lens polished before the salt dried on it. Every morning he climbed the one hundred and fourteen iron steps, counting them out of habit, and wrote the weather in the log in a hand that had shrunk a little each decade. Nobody read the log. That was the point of it.

The autumn his wife Maud died, the relief boat stopped coming. The Board wrote that the route was no longer economic and that an automated beacon would be fitted by spring. Spring came. The beacon did not. Penhale kept the light alone through the winter, and by January he had started sleeping in the chair beside the lamp room, because the stairs had begun to feel longer than they used to. He told himself this was practical. He knew it was not entirely practical.

In February a fishing boat out of the south harbour went missing in fog. Penhale heard the engine before he saw anything, an uneven thump drifting in from the water west of the rocks. His radio had died in December. What he had was a foghorn that wheezed, a brass bell, and a lamp that could be turned faster than it was built to turn. He wound the clockwork by hand, both arms working the crank until his shoulders burned, and he rang the bell until the rope tore a strip of skin from his palm. He did not stop to bind it. Stopping was not an option.

Morning came grey and flat. The boat lay on the shingle at the bottom of the cove, its bow stove in, and three men stood on the rocks above it. One of them was waving. They had steered by the flashes, they told him later, and had been sure for an hour that the light was a ship coming to meet them. Penhale had not known the lamp reached so far. He had always assumed nobody was looking up.

The Board's letter arrived in April. It thanked him for his long service and noted that Kessock Point had been reclassified as a light of secondary importance. A relief keeper would be assigned in the autumn. Penhale read the letter twice at the kitchen table, then folded it into the log book between the pages for February. He did not feel triumphant. He felt tired, which was new, and oddly he was glad of it.

Ilse Varga came over on the first boat of summer. She was the young clerk from the mainland office, and she arrived with a case of books and a bicycle she had no use for on an island with one road. She was not what he expected. She asked to see the logs, and she read them standing up, turning each page by its edge so the paper would not crease. At the end she looked up and asked why he had recorded the water temperature every single day for thirty years when no one had required it.

"Habit," he said. Then, because that was not quite true: "Maud liked to know whether the sea was cold."

Varga nodded as though this were a perfectly reasonable answer, and perhaps it was. She offered to take the night watch for a week so he could sleep properly. He refused, then accepted, and slept for eleven hours in a bed that did not move under him. He dreamed of nothing at all, which he had not done in months.

When he woke, the lamp was already burning. The log had a new entry in her neat, slanted script: wind northwest, fair, water nine degrees. Beneath it she had written one line of her own. Keeper's watch relieved. Light maintained. Penhale put on his coat and walked down the one road to the rocks, where the fishing boat had finally been hauled up and painted a bright, unlikely red. He stood beside it until the tide came in. On the way back up he did not count the steps.

Tomas had kept the light at Gull Point for nineteen years, and in all that time the lamp had never once gone dark on his watch. He wound the clockwork every four hours, day and night, and polished the lens every Tuesday whether it needed polishing or not. The station sat on a black rock a mile off the mainland. A boat came out twice a month if the sea allowed it, and the sea allowed it a little less every year. Tomas did not mind the quiet. He minded the cold, which got into the stone and stayed there until July.

The autumn Marta left, he told nobody. Dell, who brought the supplies, noticed that the second cup on the drying rack went unused all season, and he said nothing about it, which Tomas appreciated. Marta had gone to the city with a man who sold ice from a van and promised her a flat with a window that looked onto a street. Tomas understood. A rock in the sea could not offer a street. It could offer a lamp, and he had never worked out how to say that a lamp was not enough.

Through the winter he kept the log. Wind northwest, force six. Visibility eleven miles. Lamp lit at 16:42. Nothing to report. He wrote the same things over and over, and the repetition steadied him the way the clockwork did, a small mechanism that asked for nothing except to be wound on time.

In February a storm came in with no warning, the kind the old almanac called a widow's gale. The radio hissed and died. Waves broke over the gallery rail sixty feet above the water, and the tower shook so hard the kettle walked off the stove and shattered on the floor. Tomas climbed the iron stairs with the torch clamped in his teeth. The motor had failed in the first hour, which meant the lamp would turn by weight alone, and the weights had to be hauled up the central shaft by hand every forty minutes or the light would stop.

He hauled all night. His shoulders burned and his palms split on the rope, and he counted under his breath so the rhythm would hold. Around three in the morning he saw a light answer his own far out to the south, a small yellow point rising and falling where no light should have been. He flashed his torch twice. The point flashed back, then slid behind a swell and did not come up again. He stood at the rail a long time after that, watching the water heave, until the weights ran down and he had to climb the stairs again.

At dawn the sea lay flat and grey, strewn with broken planks and a single orange buoy, and there was no boat. He wrote the entry anyway. Light sighted south, no vessel confirmed. Then he sat on the bottom step with the logbook in his lap and wept, which he had not done since his father's funeral. He did it without embarrassment. There was nobody out there to be embarrassed in front of, and the gulls did not care.

Dell came out on the fourteenth with the fortnightly crates and found Tomas asleep in the chair, boots still on, the log open across his knees. Dell read the last entry twice before he woke him. A trawler called the Ardent Mary had gone missing two nights before. Her crew had been picked up that morning by a tanker, cold and half drowned, after six hours in a lifeboat that drifted toward the only landmark in the dark. The skipper said he had steered by a light on a rock, and nobody aboard could tell him which rock.

Tomas did not feel like a hero. He felt tired, and under the tiredness something quieter, like a weight he had hauled for months finally settling onto its base. He wound the clock that evening, same as every evening. Then he took the second cup down from the rack, rinsed off the salt, and set it on the table. He could not say whether Marta would ever write. He could say the cup would be there if anyone came out on the boat wanting tea and a place to sit.
